correctness.rationale: At equilibrium the renewal-reward formula gives age density P(T>a)/μ even for atomic T. Two independent age draws yield the Hilbert–Schmidt kernel cos^(2N)(Ω(A−A′)); expanding it gives nonnegative binomial weights on |m_k|² with the asserted normalization. The exponential integral up to T is Fubini-integrable because E T is finite; |m_k|≤1/(|k|Ωμ). Ratios of central binomial coefficients are bounded by one and tend to one at each fixed k, giving the limit by dominated convergence. Parseval on the period τ with normalized Fourier coefficients τ⁻¹m_k gives τ∫g². For any N≥1 the k=1 term is present; E exp(2iΩT)=1 forces phase one almost surely, so equality in either bound requires positive multiples of τ. Bracketing a mean μ≥τ by neighboring positive multiples realizes equality. For μ<τ, putting mass p=(μ−ε)/(τ−ε) at τ and the remaining mass at ε gives the mean, with A−1=ε(τ−μ)²/[μ²(τ−ε)] by the two-level density, tending to zero. The finite-purity excess divided by the central binomial bound is at most A−1. The wrapped exponential density r exp(−ra)/(1−exp(−rτ)) gives rτ coth(rτ/2)/2 upon integration of its square, confirming the benchmark. None of the argument requires convergence from a synchronized start.

value.rationale: The invariant is the loss of global purity under one common random age, not entanglement or a sum of individual-spin entropies. The exact leading constant separates arbitrary clock laws at the same mean, and the one-period cutoff explains when a physically natural strict-positive-interval constraint allows the most mixed stationary phase distribution. The many-qubit constant and the attained-versus-unattained boundary, rather than the binomial specialization alone, are the substantive contributions.
residual_risks: The threshold depends on the admissible class, especially allowing arbitrarily short positive intervals when μ<τ. It gives no indication of optimal hardware-constrained clocks or interacting-spin dynamics.
